claims.text: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a thin, uniform copper layer by vapor deposition significantly improves W–Cu interfacial bonding.
Vapor-deposited copper coatings yield near-perfect contact between tungsten and copper.
Near-perfect W–Cu contact minimizes void formation.
Near-perfect W–Cu contact minimizes phase segregation.
Reducing voids and phase segregation enhances thermal transport while maintaining mechanical durability in fusion-reactor joints.
W–Cu composites produced by mechanical alloying or spark-plasma sintering can suffer from interfacial voids.
W–Cu composites produced by mechanical alloying or spark-plasma sintering can suffer from phase inhomogeneity.
Tungsten melts at approximately 3422 °C.
Copper melts at approximately 1085 °C.
Copper boils at approximately 2562 °C.
The proposed coating creates a continuous nanoscale copper interlayer on tungsten particle surfaces.
A continuous nanoscale copper interlayer eliminates gaps at W–Cu interfaces.
The copper coating improves copper wettability on tungsten.
The copper coating promotes rapid and uniform interdiffusion during sintering.
Improved wettability and interdiffusion enhance W–Cu interfacial bonding and reduce voids and phase separation.
Reduced voids and phase separation create more continuous thermal-conduction pathways.
Relative to identically consolidated uncoated tungsten powder, vapor-coated tungsten will produce lower void content and greater microstructural uniformity.
Relative to identically consolidated uncoated tungsten powder, vapor-coated tungsten will produce higher thermal conductivity.
The vapor-coated composite will retain its mechanical performance under simulated fusion irradiation.
Filling tungsten architectures with molten or powdered copper and spark-plasma sintering without prior coating are prone to phase separation and void defects.
